question: What are Apple's main risk factors?
ground_truth: Apple's risk factors include supply chain risks such as delayed or constrained component supply and outsourcing partner shipment delays; design and manufacturing defects in products and services; service quality issues including outages, slowdowns and errors; gross margin volatility from industry pricing pressures, competition and supply shortages; foreign exchange rate impacts; data privacy and online safety compliance obligations; and antitrust and competition-law regulatory risks including the EU Digital Markets Act.
answer: Apple's main risk factors include intense competition in global markets characterized by aggressive pricing, rapid technological change, and competitors imitating its products and intellectual property [1][4][5][6]. The Company faces supply chain risks due to reliance on single or limited sources for critical components, exposure to industry-wide shortages, and dependence on outsourcing partners primarily located in Asia [1][4][5][6]. Regulatory risks include increasing data protection laws, privacy regulations, and potential penalties for non-compliance with evolving global requirements [2]. Financial risks involve fluctuating quarterly sales, gross margin pressures from pricing competition and component costs, and dependence on foreign exchange rates impacting profitability [2][6]. Business interruptions from natural disasters, geopolitical tensions (e.g., U.S.-China trade disputes), public health crises (e.g., pandemics), or supply chain disruptions could materially adversely affect operations [4][5][6]. Risks related to product development include challenges in successfully introducing new products, managing production ramps, ensuring market acceptance, and addressing quality issues [4][5]. Intellectual property risks involve potential infringement by competitors and inconsistent protection across jurisdictions [1][5]. Macroeconomic factors, such as global recessions, inflation, or credit constraints, could reduce consumer demand and disrupt supply chains [6]. Additionally, the Company’s reliance on a concentrated customer base for certain trade receivables and limited control over outsourced manufacturing and logistics pose further risks [5][6].

Markets and Distribution
The Company’s customers are primarily in the consumer, small and mid-sized business, education, enterprise and government markets. The Company sells its products and resells third-party products in most of its major markets directly to customers through its retail and online stores and its direct sales force. The Company sells its services in the same markets through its various service platforms. The Company also employs a variety of indirect distribution channels, such as third-party cellular network carriers and other resellers, for the sale of its products and certain of its services. Competition
The markets for the Company’s products and services are highly competitive and are characterized by aggressive price competition, downward pressure on gross margins, continual improvement in product performance, and price sensitivity on the part of consumers and businesses. The markets in which the Company competes are further defined by frequent introduction of new products and services, short product life cycles, evolving industry standards, and rapid adoption of technological advancements by competitors. Many of the Company’s competitors seek to compete primarily through aggressive pricing and very low cost structures, and by imitating the Company’s products and infringing on its intellectual property.

The Company also expects competition to intensify as competitors imitate the Company’s approach to providing components seamlessly within their offerings or work collaboratively to offer integrated solutions. Some of the Company’s competitors have broad product lines, low-priced products, large installed bases of active devices, and large customer bases. Competition has been particularly intense as competitors have aggressively cut prices and lowered product margins. The Company also competes for various components with other participants in the markets for smartphones, personal computers, tablets, wearables and accessories. Therefore, many components used by the Company, including those that are available from multiple sources, are at times subject to industry-wide shortage and significant commodity pricing fluctuations. Restrictions on international trade can increase the cost or limit the availability of the Company’s products and the components and rare earths and other raw materials that go into them.
The Company uses some custom components that are not commonly used by its competitors, and new products introduced by the Company often utilize custom components available from only one source. When a component or product uses new technologies, initial capacity constraints may exist until the suppliers’ yields have matured or their manufacturing capacities have increased. The Company has entered into agreements for the supply of many components; however, the Company may not be able to extend or renew agreements for the supply of components on similar terms, or at all, and may not be successful in obtaining sufficient quantities from its suppliers or in a timely manner, or in identifying and obtaining sufficient quantities from an alternative source. Over time, the Company has accumulated a large portfolio of issued and registered intellectual property rights around the world. No single intellectual property right is solely responsible for protecting the Company’s products and services. The Company is subject to an increasing number of federal, state and international laws relating to the collection, use, retention, security and transfer of various types of personal information. In many cases, these laws apply not only to third-party transactions, but also restrict transfers of personal information among the Company and its international subsidiaries. These laws continue to develop and may be inconsistent from jurisdiction to jurisdiction. Complying with emerging and changing requirements causes the Company to incur substantial costs and has required and may in the future require the Company to change its business practices. Noncompliance could result in significant penalties or legal liability.
The Company makes statements about its use and disclosure of personal information through its privacy policy, information provided on its website, press statements and other privacy notices provided to customers. Any failure by the Company to comply with these public statements or with federal, state or international privacy or data protection laws and regulations could result in inquiries or proceedings against the Company by governmental entities or others. In addition to reputational impacts, penalties could include ongoing audit requirements and significant legal liability.
In addition to the risks generally relating to the collection, use, retention, security and transfer of personal information, the Company is also subject to specific obligations relating to information considered sensitive under applicable laws, such as health data, financial data and biometric data. Health data and financial data are subject to additional privacy, security and breach notification requirements, and the Company is subject to audit by governmental authorities regarding the Company’s compliance with these obligations. If the Company fails to adequately comply with these rules and requirements, or if health data or financial data is handled in a manner not permitted by law or under the Company’s agreements with healthcare or financial institutions, the Company can be subject to litigation or government investigations, and can be liable for associated investigatory expenses, and can also incur significant fees or fines.
Payment card data is also subject to additional requirements. Under payment card rules and obligations, if cardholder information is potentially compromised, the Company can be liable for associated investigatory expenses and can also incur significant fees or fines if the Company fails to follow payment card industry data security standards. Additionally, strengthening of foreign currencies may increase the Company’s cost of product components denominated in those currencies, thus adversely affecting gross margins.
The Company uses derivative instruments, such as foreign currency forward and option contracts, to hedge certain exposures to fluctuations in foreign exchange rates. question: How does the EU Digital Markets Act affect Apple?
ground_truth: Apple is subject to the EU Digital Markets Act (DMA) and has a compliance plan intended to address the DMA's obligations, engaging with the European Commission. Noncompliance could result in significant fines and required changes to business practices.
answer: The EU Digital Markets Act (DMA) requires Apple to implement changes in its EU operations, including new business terms, alternative fee structures for iOS and iPadOS apps, alternative distribution methods, alternative payment processing, and additional tools and APIs for developers [1][2]. Apple has faced investigations and penalties under the DMA, including a €500 million fine from the European Commission in April 2025 for restricting developers’ ability to promote alternative distribution channels, which the Company has appealed [3]. The Commission has also opened additional investigations under Articles 5(4) and 6(4) of the DMA, with potential fines up to 10% of Apple’s annual worldwide net sales if violations are found [3][4]. Compliance with the DMA exposes Apple to risks such as reduced privacy and security for EU users, potential further changes to business practices, and material adverse effects on its business, reputation, results of operations, and financial condition [1][2]. The DMA’s requirements and enforcement actions could also lead to ongoing litigation and challenges from regulators and private litigants, increasing legal and operational costs [2][3].

question: Why do Apple's gross margins fluctuate?
ground_truth: Apple's gross margins vary significantly across products, services, geographic segments and distribution channels and are subject to volatility and downward pressure from factors including industry-wide pricing pressures, competition, product life cycles, supply shortages, and component costs.
answer:
Apple's gross margins fluctuate due to a variety of factors, including:  

1. **Industry-wide global product pricing pressures and competitive actions** that the Company may take in response, which can reduce margins [1][2].  
2. **Increased competition**, which exerts downward pressure on pricing and margins [1][2].  
3. **The Company’s ability to effectively stimulate demand** for certain products and services, as lower demand can reduce sales volume and margin performance [1][2].  
4. **Compressed product life cycles**, which may shorten the period during which products generate higher margins [1][2].  
5. **Supply shortages**, which can increase costs or disrupt production, affecting margins [1][2].  
6. **Potential increases in the cost of components, outside manufacturing services, and content development/delivery** for services, which directly impact cost of sales [1][2].  
7. **The Company’s ability to manage product quality and warranty costs effectively**, as higher warranty expenses can reduce gross margins [1][2].  
8. **Shifts in the mix of products and services**, as different products and services have varying profit margins (e.g., Pro models vs. other iPhones) [1][2][5].  
9. **Changes in geographic, currency, or channel mix**, including regulatory changes requiring modifications to product offerings, which alter revenue and cost structures [1][2][5].  
10. **Fluctuations in foreign exchange rates**, which affect the U.S. dollar value of foreign currency-denominated sales and costs. For example, weakening foreign currencies relative to the U.S. dollar may lead to higher international pricing (reducing demand) or lower U.S. dollar gross margins if pricing is not adjusted [1][2][4].  
11. **Inflation and other macroeconomic pressures**, which increase operational and input costs [1][2].  
12. **The introduction of new products or services with lower profit margins**, such as new product launches that initially carry lower margins [1][2].  
13. **Tariffs and trade restrictions**, which can increase costs or reduce demand, impacting gross margins [2][5].  

Specific examples from financial performance include:  
- In 2025, **Products gross margin increased** due to favorable costs and a different product mix but was **partially offset by tariff costs** [5].  
- In 2024, **Products gross margin increased** due to cost savings but was **partially offset by a different product mix and the weakness of foreign currencies** relative to the U.S. dollar [4].  
- **Services gross margin** has increased in recent years due to higher net sales and shifts in the mix of services (e.g., growth in advertising, App Store, and cloud services) [4][5].  

These factors, among others, contribute to the volatility and downward pressure on Apple’s gross margins [1][2].

ground_truth: Apple's sales are affected by holiday seasonal demand, with higher net sales in its first fiscal quarter.
answer: Apple has historically experienced higher net sales in its first fiscal quarter compared to other quarters due in part to seasonal holiday demand [1][2]. question: What antitrust lawsuits does Apple face in the United States?
ground_truth: Apple is subject to civil antitrust lawsuits in the U.S. alleging monopolization or attempted monopolization in the markets for performance smartphones and smartphones generally in violation of U.S. antitrust laws.
answer:
Apple faces civil antitrust lawsuits in the U.S. alleging monopolization or attempted monopolization in the markets for “performance smartphones” and “smartphones” generally under U.S. antitrust laws [1]. Specifically, on March 21, 2024, the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) and several state and district attorneys general filed a civil antitrust lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey against Apple, seeking equitable relief to address alleged anticompetitive behavior [3]. Additionally, various civil litigation matters have been filed in U.S. state and federal courts alleging similar violations of U.S. antitrust laws and seeking monetary damages and other nonmonetary relief [3].  

Separately, Epic Games, Inc. filed a lawsuit against Apple in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, alleging violations of federal and state antitrust laws and California’s unfair competition law related to Apple’s App Store practices. The court found that certain provisions of Apple’s App Store Review Guidelines violated California’s unfair competition law and issued an injunction prohibiting Apple from blocking developers from including external links to alternative purchasing mechanisms in their apps [3].  

These lawsuits, among others, expose Apple to potential fines, business practice changes, and reputational harm if resolved unfavorably [1][3].

Summary of Significant Accounting Policies
Basis of Presentation and Preparation
The consolidated financial statements include the accounts of Apple Inc. and its wholly owned subsidiaries. The preparation of these consolidated financial statements and accompanying notes in conformity with GAAP requires the use of management estimates. Certain prior period amounts in the notes to consolidated financial statements have been reclassified to conform to the current period’s presentation.
The Company’s fiscal year is the 52- or 53-week period that ends on the last Saturday of September. An additional week is included in the first fiscal quarter every five or six years to realign the Company’s fiscal quarters with calendar quarters, which occurred in the first fiscal quarter of 2023. The Company’s fiscal years 2025 and 2024 spanned 52 weeks each, whereas fiscal year 2023 spanned 53 weeks. Unless otherwise stated, references to particular years, quarters, months and periods refer to the Company’s fiscal years ended in September and the associated quarters, months and periods of those fiscal years.
Recently Adopted Accounting Pronouncements
Segment Reporting
Beginning with the 2025 annual reporting period, the Company adopted the FASB’s ASU No. 2023-07, 
Segment Reporting (Topic 280): Improvements to Reportable Segment Disclosures 
(“ASU 2023-07”), which requires the Company to disclose segment expenses that are significant and regularly provided to the Company’s chief operating decision maker (“CODM”). In addition, ASU 2023-07 requires the Company to disclose the title and position of its CODM and how the CODM uses segment profit or loss information in assessing segment performance and deciding how to allocate resources. The Company adopted ASU 2023-07 using a retrospective transition method.
Revenue
The Company records revenue net of taxes collected from customers that are remitted to governmental authorities.
Share-Based Compensation
The Company recognizes share-based compensation expense on a straight-line basis for its estimate of equity awards that will ultimately vest.
Cash Equivalents
All highly liquid investments with maturities of three months or less at the date of purchase are treated as cash equivalents.
